rv.q: It is all beautiful, brilliant, maniacally unmissable.
Sarah Snook triumphs in this game-changing piece of theatre
And this is a virtuoso performance in an astonishing piece of theatre.

This is an exceptional and unusual piece of work that also presents Snook’s Dorian as a prototype TikTok influencer - editing her face on a mobile phone for plumper lips, longer lashes and bionic eyebrows - and bringing this cautionary tale bang up to date, in form and content.
Whether you enjoy this show as a star vehicle, a Wildean debate on morality versus self-expression, or a cutting-edge piece of mixed-media art, it’s an extraordinary event.

This version, conceived and directed by Kip Williams for Australia’s Sydney Theatre Company, frolics in Wilde’s purple prose without becoming smothered by it, to become its own brilliantly unhinged, camp creation.
It unfurls into a truly dazzling technical construct, a trippy, doomy two hour odyssey.
It's a riveting piece of storytelling... an astonishing feat, and Snook magics Wilde's lurid yarn into high-definition life.
This impeccable technological feat, so fraught with potential peril, unfolds without a single glitch.
Williams’s production is a surprising thing, full of magical transformations, sensory splendour and technical ingenuity.
This show may be a glimpse of the technological future of theatre, but as storytelling, it’s old hat.
This form-bending, innovative feat of a production and performance will have your jaw on the floor.
It’s unlike anything currently on stage on the West End.

Williams’ staging of his own adaptation opens with a fierce close-up of Snook’s exuberant face on a large, portrait-style screen — the first of many — hanging down at the center of the proscenium arch.
This is incredibly ambitious staging that pays off in spades.
At the heart of all this stands Snook, who is utterly superb.
This "Picture of Dorian Gray" is, on its own terms, a triumph.
This show is a lightweight pastiche, like a French & Saunders spoof, but it lacks the substance for a whole evening’s entertainment.
Absolutely phenomenal in every way – from Sarah Snook’s astonishing acting to Kip Williams’ dynamic direction, this production of The Picture of Dorian Gray is a work of art.
I loved this show even as I was frustrated by it.

cn.t: Critics hail Sarah Snook's virtuosic one-woman performance as stunning and audacious, with Williams' tech-heavy adaptation praised as a dazzling, innovative spectacle. A few find it gimmicky or overpriced, but most celebrate this camp, multimedia reimagining.
